lenders.role: Loan IBRD-77460, written L7746-YF, of US$388 million for the Corridor X Highway Project (P108005), approved 9 July 2009 and effective 6 November 2009, with additional financing IBRD-86550 of US$38.9 million approved 25 October 2016. US$335,213,259 was disbursed on the first loan and US$40,340,629 on the second. The original closing date of 31 December 2015 was extended twice and actual closing was 30 September 2019. The borrower was to contribute US$60 million and contributed US$7.24 million; total project cost at appraisal was US$486.9 million against US$382,793,888 actual. The loan financed motorway sections on E-75 and E-80: the Dimitrovgrad bypass on E-80, Grabovnica-Grdelica and Vladicin Han-Donji Neradovac on E-75, with Lot 6, the Manajle-Vladicin Han tunnel, added in 2014. The company gave no official response to N1's questions in November 2016; its representatives had visited the village and promised that all damage would be compensated once blasting was finally over.

corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.community: The loan paid for motorway sections on Corridor X, including the bypass around Dimitrovgrad on the E-80 towards the Bulgarian border. The appraisal document of 12 June 2009 expected expropriation on the Bank-financed sections of 50 hectares on Grabovnica-Grdelica, 130 hectares on Vladicin Han-Donji Neradovac and 50 hectares on the 8.67 kilometres around Dimitrovgrad, 230 hectares in all. The completion report records land acquisition of 322.7 hectares across 2,092 cases on those three sections, rising to 371.8 hectares and 2,491 cases once Lot 6 was added, and says there were delays in complying with the resettlement action plans because of the slow expropriation process in 2011-2012 and in 2015, caused by a lack of expropriation funds, disputes over expropriation, and delays in paying subsistence and transitional allowances to displaced families. It states that the expropriation process for the whole project was substantially completed by 2016 and that the handling of expropriation impacts was consistent with the Bank-endorsed plans and complied with the resettlement policy. An end-of-term impact evaluation of resettlement on the Dimitrovgrad bypass, dated 12 July 2016, goes further. The resettlement action plan recorded 33 structures expropriated and compensated on that section; the road enterprise's own records held 30 cases, the difference being that some cases bundled a house with its wells, fences and storage. Thirteen cases included houses and only three of those involved physical relocation: six of the seven residential structures recorded at Dimitrovgrad were weekend houses, one house was derelict with nobody living in it, and three of the six houses at Gradinje were weekend homes. The evaluation interviewed representatives of two of the three physically displaced households. One had bought a new house, smaller than the old one, with compensation of RSD 7,630,169, about EUR 85,000, covering a 4,497 square metre plot and the structures, and the evaluation judged that adequate and above local market prices. The second, who declined to take part, had received about EUR 70,000 for structures. In neither case was there evidence that the moving allowance the law prescribes or the transitional allowance the resettlement policy framework requires had been paid. The third case was a household and a business together. Vasil Kolev had a 140 square metre building at Gradinje with a registered car repair workshop on the ground floor and the family home above; it was fully expropriated and the replacement value was assessed at about EUR 27,000, or EUR 160 a square metre. He was notified in 2008, was not satisfied with the valuation, and says the authorities did not respond to his appeal to reassess. He received no moving allowance, no transitional allowance and no compensation for loss of business or loss of income; the valuation covered the construction value of the workshop only, so the equipment in it was not valued, and he removed it himself at his own cost. Losing the workshop left the household without its only source of income. He was 60 at the time of the interview, worked part time as a handyman, and lived with his wife, disabled from birth, and a daughter trained as a hairdresser but not in full-time work. He said property prices in Dimitrovgrad had risen since the expropriation began and he could not buy a new property, and that he lives in a house inherited from his father. The evaluation confirmed from the valuation report that only the construction value had been assessed, found that the basic requirements of the resettlement policy framework had not been met in his case, recommended that the outstanding allowances be paid retrospectively to the displaced households and that an independent review of his case be carried out, and noted that he had since claimed to have the property expropriated back because the building had never been demolished and a slight change to the carriageway alignment made demolition unlikely. The expropriation of these households was completed in Phase 1, in 2008 and 2009, before the international lenders came into the project. The appraisal document had said as much in advance about an adjoining stretch: expropriation on the first 5.9 kilometres from Prosek towards Crvena Reka began in late 2008 and, although the Bank reviewed the process, that section was not to be subject to the policies set out in the resettlement policy framework. The construction impacts were not. Negative impacts the affected people reported during the works were damage to local roads, limited access to land parcels, effects on the value of utilities, and blasting. The evaluation records the municipality's representatives as stating that over 100 households were affected to varying extents by the blasting and that about 20 households at Gradinje were severely affected. Eleven households had been identified as vulnerable when the resettlement plan was prepared and each received additional financial assistance of RSD 60,000. Court appeals were brought over compensation for lost crops; the evaluation found no records of how many crop expropriation cases there were, because all records sat in paper case files, and no information on the court cases or their outcomes, and concluded that the appeals were not non-compliance with the plan or a major impact. N1 reported on 24 November 2016 from the village of Gradina near Dimitrovgrad that construction was going on a few metres from houses, that it had run about five years, that houses had cracks inside and out which residents attributed to the blasting and the works, and that residents whose houses were damaged were waiting for compensation. It reported that residents had written to several authorities asking to be relocated, had written again the week before, and had threatened to block the blasting. One of them, Nebojsa Ivanov, said that experts had come and had said the building was not safe to live in, and that he would have to sue if he could not reach an agreement with Koridori Srbije. One resident, Nebojsa Ivanov, said: 'Nista ne kazu. Kao da ne postojimo' - they say nothing, as if we do not exist. Another resident, Slavka Gligorijev, said she was waiting for the works to end and did not know what would be done about the damaged houses. The report said at least five firms had worked on the section over the five years and residents had asked all of them for compensation, but the damage only grew; and that unofficially, expropriation would not happen at this stage and residents with damaged houses would have to wait for compensation until all work was finished. Koridori Srbije gave no official response. The evaluation's own view of the wider picture was that Dimitrovgrad remains one of the poorest municipalities in Serbia, that the affected people's perception of their economic position was negative but that they attributed the worsening to factors outside the project, and that there had been observable improvement in their socio-economic conditions since 2009, some of it from compensation money and construction jobs.
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.displaced_label: Households physically displaced on the Dimitrovgrad bypass section, from the end-of-term impact evaluation of resettlement of 12 July 2016
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,337 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 2,491 cases of affected landowners across 371.8 hectares for the whole project and gives no count of people relocated. The three is for the Dimitrovgrad bypass section alone, the only section with a published end-of-term resettlement evaluation; no equivalent count was found for the E-75 sections, where the completion report records delays in paying subsistence and transitional allowances to displaced families without saying how many families.
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.suppression: Vasil Kolev told the evaluation's consultant that when he sought legal assistance from several lawyers, none of them would represent him, on the pretext that it is better not to go against the State. The evaluation reports this as his statement and does not name the lawyers or test the claim.
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.killed_note: The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that there were three fatalities during highway construction. The completion report records three separate fatal accidents at the sites - in September 2013 at Grabovnica-Grdelica and in November 2014 and February 2017 at the Dimitrovgrad bypass - and attributes them to unsatisfactory management of site safety; a health and safety audit report and a site safety action plan were implemented for the first two and additional safety measures introduced for the third. The review says that apart from stating unsatisfactory management of site safety the completion report gives no detail on whether the safety measures were sufficient to protect construction workers, whether there was negligence, and whether the accidents could have been avoided. Neither document names the people killed or says what each accident was.
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2019, almost four years after its original date, with the Bank-financed sections open to traffic. The end-of-term evaluation of 12 July 2016 recommended that the outstanding moving and transitional allowances be paid retrospectively to the displaced households, that an independent review of Vasil Kolev's case be carried out, that the scale of construction impacts on the community be verified and documented and that outstanding compensation be paid in full. On the blasting damage the evaluation records that compensation was being paid by the insurer Wiener Stadtische but that only five cases had been compensated by the time it was written and that the claim process was long, and that the damage to houses in and around Sutjeska Street in Dimitrovgrad was reimbursed for five households out of the contractor's bank guarantee on court decisions, with further cases pending in court. No document found records how many households were compensated in the end, whether the evaluation's recommendations were acted on, or how Vasil Kolev's claim to have the property expropriated back was resolved. The completion report of 24 March 2020 rated the outcome Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed, while downrating Bank performance to Moderately Satisfactory over the three construction deaths.

corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.confidence_note: The three physically displaced households, the missing moving and transitional allowances, the uncompensated loss of the car repair workshop and the over 100 households affected by blasting all come from the end-of-term impact evaluation of resettlement, a field study commissioned by the state company that ran the works and published by the Bank. That is not an independent document: the evaluator was engaged by the implementing entity. N1's report of 24 November 2016 corroborates independently that houses near the works were cracked, that residents attributed this to blasting, and that compensation was being withheld until the works finished, and it names two residents, one of whom states that experts had found his building unsafe to live in. The report does not say who engaged those experts. N1 places its report in the village of Gradina while the evaluation's affected structures are at Gradinje and Dimitrovgrad; both villages lie on the same bypass section, and no document found states that they are the same place. The expropriation of the three displaced households, including the workshop, was completed in 2008 and 2009, before the international lenders joined the project; what falls inside the loan period is the construction impact, the Bank-endorsed resettlement framework under which the allowances were owed, and the evaluation's finding that they had not been paid. Vasil Kolev's account of his losses, and the statement that lawyers would not represent him, are his own, recorded by the evaluation's consultant, who confirmed from the valuation report only that the workshop had been valued for construction value alone and noted that no evidence was provided of how the business operated or how much income was lost. The completion report states the opposite conclusion on the same facts - that the handling of expropriation impacts complied with the resettlement policy - and the evaluation found the compensation paid to the displaced households adequate and above local market prices. The three construction deaths are counted by the Independent Evaluation Group; neither document names the people killed, says what happened in each accident, or says whether the deaths could have been avoided. No document found gives the number of households whose houses cracked or what they were paid in total; the evaluation records five cases compensated by the works insurer and five households compensated out of the contractor's bank guarantee on court decisions, with further cases pending. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 8 October 2020 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is unverified at document level.
corridor-x-dimitrovgrad-bypass-serbia.conditions: The project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). A resettlement policy framework was prepared for the whole project and disclosed on 4 June 2009, with separate resettlement action plans for the Dimitrovgrad bypass (April 2010), Grabovnica-Grdelica (July 2011), Vladicin Han-Donji Neradovac (April 2012, with an annex in March 2014) and the Lot 6 Manajle-Vladicin Han tunnel (April 2014), and an addendum in May 2015. Two corridor-level environmental impact assessments covering the whole of E-75 and E-80 were cleared before appraisal in May 2009, with seven sub-section assessments for E-75 and five for E-80 consolidated into them, and site-specific environmental management plans issued with the bidding documents for each works contract. Serbian expropriation law requires affected structures to be compensated at full replacement cost, treats a partly affected structure as wholly expropriated, and provides for a moving allowance in cases of physical relocation but prescribes no transitional allowance; the resettlement policy framework required a transitional allowance as well. The end-of-term evaluation of 12 July 2016 found that the framework's basic requirements had not been met in the case of the affected business, that there was no evidence that the moving or transitional allowances had been paid to any of the three physically displaced households, and that the monitoring of construction impacts the resettlement plan required was not a priority in the contractors' obligations (End of Term Impact Evaluation of Resettlement, 12 July 2016; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 March 2020).

milot-rreshen-road-compensation-albania.community: The loan and credit paid for 26 kilometres of road between Milot and Rreshen, built in three lots and all open to traffic by the project's close. The completion report names the Milot-Rreshen section as the main project activity that triggered land acquisition, and records that a resettlement action plan was prepared by the road agency's project implementation team and approved by the Bank. Land was acquired in two rounds. After the first was finished, the Government enacted a new Law on Property Valuation in 2010, which changed how compensation was calculated and, in the completion report's words, 'led to a reduction in the rate of compensation paid to Project-affected persons'. The change was made to accommodate a redesign of the road alignment and an unrelated landslip in Fang village. The Bank team, after taking advice from its regional safeguards adviser and project lawyer, told the road agency it could apply the new law, and the resettlement action plan was changed accordingly. The report says the new law 'triggered some dissatisfaction from people who had gone through the first expropriation and then through the second'. Payment of compensation was also delayed. Some title holders were out of the country or had died with successors who held no title. The 2010 law required compensation to be paid through one named bank; most of the people affected by the construction works lived in the area where the flood protection works were built and were rural, and many had no bank account, so the report states that this provision 'significantly delayed payments of due compensations'. The project implementation team explained an alternative method of calculating compensation, had land registration offices give owners without titles preferential status, helped every owner open an account at the nearest branch of the designated bank in Milot, Rrubik or Rreshen, and opened an escrow account for those who had died or were abroad. Twenty-three households lost their homes and had to be relocated; all were compensated and assisted to settle in new places, and in one case where the residence was occupied without title the Municipality of Milot provided the family with a new apartment at no cost. A further 12 households lost their commercial structures in part or in whole. Three hundred and thirty-eight households lost agricultural or commercial land. Compensation for residential and commercial structures totalled ALL 174,165,661, about US$1.7 million, and compensation for agricultural and commercial land and for lost agricultural production and expected income in the year of taking and the two or three years after came to ALL 185,854,139, about US$1.8 million. The completion report states that all compensation was fully paid to the people affected by the end of the project.

milot-rreshen-road-compensation-albania.outcome: The loan and credit closed on 30 June 2011 on their original date, with all three lots of the 26 kilometre road complete and open to traffic. The report does not say how many people had received compensation at the reduced rate set by the 2010 law, how much less they received than under the earlier method, or how long the delayed payments took.

milot-rreshen-road-compensation-albania.confidence_note: Every figure here - the 23 households relocated, the 12 that lost commercial structures, the 338 that lost land, the two compensation totals, the reduction in the compensation rate and the significant delay in payments - comes from the Bank's own completion report, which reports the road agency's figures. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report adds no resettlement detail. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of these expropriations was found in Albanian-language or other sources. The report states that the reduction in the compensation rate followed from a change in national law that the Bank told the agency it could apply, not from a failure by the agency. It also states that all compensation was fully paid by the end of the project, that the relocated households were compensated and assisted to settle, and that the affected people were in the end satisfied; that last statement is attributed to meetings with the Bank project team and direct interaction with the road agency, not to any survey or document. The report does not name any affected person, does not say how much less anyone received under the new law, and does not say how long the payment delays ran. The ICR Review carries a Date Posted line of 27 September 2013.
milot-rreshen-road-compensation-albania.conditions: The project was environmental category A. A resettlement action plan was prepared by the road agency's project implementation team and approved by the Bank, and the completion report states that it complied with Albanian law and with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy. An Environmental Unit established in the agency in early 2004, on the recommendation of an environmental management capacity assessment carried out under the previous Bank-supported road maintenance project, handled environmental compliance, and the Bank team gave it detailed guidance on applying the safeguard policies. Supervision consultants withheld payment for traffic management in any month where the contractor's provision was deemed unacceptable. When Albania enacted a new Law on Property Valuation in 2010, which changed the basis for calculating compensation and reduced the rate paid, the Bank team sought the advice of its regional safeguards adviser and project lawyer and then told the road agency that it could apply the new law, and the resettlement action plan was changed to match. The same law required compensation to be paid through one designated bank (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2011).

amman-development-corridor-land.community: The loans paid for the first 40 kilometre phase of the Amman Ring Road, running from Zarqa, Amman's main industrial suburb, past Queen Alia International Airport, and for a new customs depot and inland port at Madounah. The completion report states that the scale of land acquisition required was far greater than any land acquisition programme previously carried out in Jordan. The number of people ultimately affected, defined as owners and occupants who lost some of their land, housing or other physical assets, was 3,028, and compensation payments amounted to about US$160 million equivalent, against the US$158.43 million the report's own cost table gives. Three quarters of the compensation, covering 440 hectares, 850 plots and 2,250 affected people, was for the 40 kilometre road route; one quarter, covering 500 hectares, 240 plots and 778 affected people, was for the Madounah areas selected in 2006 for the customs depot and inland port. The draft land acquisition and resettlement plan disclosed in February 2004 had indicated the road would affect about 500 plots with about 1,900 identified owners, the very large majority private parties. Particular attention was given to people considered vulnerable: female landowners, who were about a third of those identified; tenants; people dependent on customary rights, mainly herders whose livelihoods came almost entirely from the rangelands the road runs through; and the 300 or so owners and occupants who had to find new places for themselves and their dependents to live. Because the road was to be Jordan's first limited-access facility, the Government agreed to pay each owner for all the land taken rather than the 75 per cent that Jordanian law permits and that earlier public requisitions had applied. An independent monitor was appointed and reviewed the programme at the turn of 2006 and 2007, later than intended because of difficulty finding a suitable expert. She carried out physical and telephone interviews, reached broadly positive conclusions, called the approach 'an exemplary approach to be pursued in similar future projects', and identified areas for improvement, chiefly more follow-up with affected people after their land had been given up and better recording of their contacts with officials. In response the ministry's community liaison office interviewed a sample of affected people, especially women and those physically resettled. The completion report states that those interview reports 'record widespread concern particularly about the slow payment of compensation - with eight months seeming to be found often acceptable, but not periods well in excess of one year as seem to have arisen not too often but nonetheless more frequently than expected'. The period of compensation payment and resettlement, 2004 to 2008, coincided with large increases in the price of land and building materials, driven by oil price rises, the removal of earlier subsidies and the arrival of people fleeing the fighting in Iraq. Other interviews recorded the ministry responding flexibly to cases that risked severe harm: watering roads to reduce dust that was damaging olive harvests, building additional animal underpasses to reconnect herders' grazing lands, small changes to the road alignment to avoid taking small pieces of property, and measures to speed up payment to people in exceptional difficulty. At Madounah, the 500 hectares were acquired at the chosen intersection for the customs depot and inland port, and were not in the 2004 project cost estimates. In 2006 the Government announced a Mafraq Special Development Zone closer to the Syrian border and work on designing an inland port was abruptly suspended; in 2008 further development of the new customs depot was suspended as well, because the Army decided at that time to build a medical centre at Madounah. That plan was never carried out either. The completion report states that no development has occurred on the lands acquired at Madounah beyond the land levelling, advance works and bulk utility supply lines done in 2005 and 2006, that the customs depot has not moved from its congested site at the edge of the city, and that the Ministry of Transport and the Customs Department verbally confirmed that the depot and logistics platform might still be built there, but without any official written decision.
amman-development-corridor-land.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,898 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report gives 3,028 people affected, defined as owners and occupants who lost land, housing or other physical assets, and separately refers to 'the 300 or so owners/occupants who had to find new places for their dependents and themselves to live'. That 300 is approximate in the document and no exact count of people relocated was found. No document found gives an exact number of people relocated.
amman-development-corridor-land.outcome: The loans closed on 31 December 2012, three and a half years late. lagos-brt-ikorodu-market-traders.community: The credit paid for reconstructing the Mile 12 to Ikorodu road from four lanes to six with a bus rapid transit corridor, 13.5 kilometres of it, plus 3.55 kilometres of Akin Adesola and Wempco Roads, the Ikeja bus terminal and the Ojota bus depot. Resettlement action plans were prepared, reviewed and disclosed for the affected sites along the Mile 12 to Ikorodu and Mile 12 to Tafawa Balewa Square corridors and for the Ikeja terminal and Ojota depot. The completion report states that land acquired along the corridors and at the other sites affected 2,231 individuals and that all were compensated appropriately as planned, and its footnote breaks that down: 473 at Ikorodu, 572 at Ikorodu Market, 134 at Agric, 15 at Ogolonto, 55 at Ajegunle, 40 at Owode Section, 75 at Owode Market and 867 at Mile 12. Three groups were still unsettled when the credit closed on 31 May 2017, which is why social safeguards were rated Moderately Satisfactory. Street traders at Ikorodu roundabout were to be moved to the Oluwo Oduikan Market at Agric, built under the project, to improve traffic flow and safety around Ikorodu station. From 2016 some of them moved back to trade near the station on their own initiative; the implementing agency convened meetings in February and March 2017 with the state ministry, the local government, the Markets Board, the Markets Association, the traders and the traditional institution to agree a timeline, and the affected traders then refused to comply in May 2017. After the credit closed, Ikorodu West Council Development took over running the new market, met the stakeholders again and reached an agreement under which the traders moved into the Agric market, which is operational. A group of plantain market traders had been moved from the Mile 12 terminal site to the nearby Ajelogo market under a three-year lease. The lease expired in 2017 and they had to move again. They petitioned the World Bank in April 2017. After the credit closed, the State Ministry of Local Government and Community Affairs led a reconciliation that ended in September 2017 in an official agreement, signed by all the parties, under which the state would move them to a permanent site at Imota in Ikorodu once its construction was finished; the completion report says the traders expressed satisfaction with the final deal and pledged to work with the state to re-establish their livelihood. Eight of the people identified in the Ikeja bus terminal resettlement plan had not collected their compensation by the closing date of 31 May 2017, and all had received it by September 2017. The implementing agency's own lessons, printed in the completion report, set out what it thought had gone wrong. Resettlement plans should be holistic, sustainable and transparent to affected people, and security of land tenure is what makes them sustainable: 'Without it, the objective of the resettlement action will be defeated and another resettlement will have to occur in the future. In the case of the Ayangbunren Market traders, PAPs were displaced from one uncertain future to another equally uncertain future. In the long run, it is doubtful whether money used to secure the resettlement brings any value.' It added that terms of agreements must be properly explained, and that where affected people are illiterate or work in a language other than English an illiterate jurat should always be inserted into the agreement so that what the person signs is shown to be understood; that resettlement should not end with allocating stalls and moving people, but needs an oversight role afterwards to sort out problems and assure the resettled people's security and tenure; and that the agency should obtain long-term leases of land on which affected people are resettled, because short-term lease tenure is not ideal, and that where land cannot be acquired by government under the Land Use Act the lease should run at least ten years with a proviso letting the market associations negotiate a further lease.
lagos-brt-ikorodu-market-traders.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,749 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 2,231 individuals affected by land acquisition along the corridors and at the other sites, broken down by site, and says all were compensated as planned. It does not give a count of how many traders were actually moved from any one market, how many moved back to Ikorodu station, or how many plantain traders were moved from the Mile 12 terminal to Ajelogo and then had to move again.
lagos-brt-ikorodu-market-traders.outcome: The credit closed on 31 May 2017 with three resettlement matters unfinished. All three were settled after closing: the Ikorodu roundabout traders moved into the Agric market, which is operational; the Mile 12 plantain traders signed an agreement in September 2017 to be moved to a permanent site at Imota in Ikorodu once its construction is complete, so at the time of the completion report they were still waiting for that site; and the eight people at the Ikeja terminal had collected their compensation by September 2017. The completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Satisfactory, on modest efficiency, 200 per cent cost overruns on the Mile 12 to Ikorodu corridor that it says cannot be fully explained by inflation and construction costs, and the cancellation of a further 27 kilometres. No document found says whether the Imota market was built or whether the plantain traders ever reached it.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits and grants IDA-43370, IDA-46590, IDA-49870, IDA-51460, IDA-H3140, IDA-H3150, IDA-H5220 and IDA-H7980 for the CEMAC Transport-Transit Facilitation Project (P079736), a regional project covering the Central African Republic, Cameroon and Chad and filed by the Bank under the country 'Central Africa' rather than under any member state. Original commitment US$201 million at approval on 26 June 2007, effective 5 December 2007, with three additional financings - US$217 million approved 5 November 2009 under P115259, US$112 million approved 23 June 2011 under P125915 and US$125 million approved 26 July 2012 under P130422. Total project cost was US$741,489,423 at appraisal, revised to US$642,633,379, with US$578,194,665 disbursed. Original closing was 31 January 2013 and actual closing 28 February 2021, after eight restructurings including two cancellations of financing in June 2020 and February 2021. The project was reclassified from environmental category B to category A in the restructuring of 31 January 2017, which also changed the project development objectives, the safeguard policies triggered, the legal covenants and the institutional arrangements. It financed the Baboua-Fambele (34 km) and Fambele-Bouar (34 km) and Baoro-Bouar (56 km) road sections in the Central African Republic, road works in Cameroon including the Mora-Dabanga-Kousseri section, a rail component with CAMRAIL, and a road station at Bouar. The completion report of 29 October 2021 rated outcome Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest, and rated the project's financial and accounting management Moderately Unsatisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 7 March 2022 agreed on outcome and on monitoring and evaluation but rated Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, citing substantial shortcomings at entry and moderate shortcomings in supervision, among them eight successive task team leaders and the Bank's reactive handling of delayed resettlement, of the severe accidents and of ineligible expenditure (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 October 2021; Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review).

The completion report records that the corps did not fully comply with labour law requirements for civilian staff, listing irregularities in affiliation to the National Social Insurance Fund, medical check-ups on hiring not always properly ensured, and non-payment of wages, and that the works were not completed, which it attributes to the corps' poor performance and to continuing insecurity that prevented subcontractors being mobilised in time. The Independent Evaluation Group calls the arrangement an innovative option chosen to address security and says the results obtained were poor, partly from the Bank's lack of experience of working in conflict areas.

companies.name: Cameroon Railways (CAMRAIL)

baoro-bouar-road-house-damage-car.community: The credits and grants paid for road and rail works along the Douala to Bangui and Douala to N'Djamena corridors, including 56 kilometres of road from Baoro to Bouar in the Central African Republic. The project was assessed as having high social risk. Resettlement action plans were prepared in the project's first phase in 2007 in all three countries, and a resettlement policy framework was prepared for Cameroon during the 2016 restructuring because of the security situation; the framework identified the need to recruit a non-governmental organisation to monitor the complaints mechanism and social communication. On the Baoro-Bouar works a local non-governmental organisation was recruited to run the grievance mechanism, replacing arrangements the contractor had set up at the start of the works before the government had engaged an organisation, and the contractor also ran a separate mechanism of its own. The completion report rates the carrying out of the grievance mechanism Satisfactory at project closing, and records what it produced. Over one year the organisation registered 1,350 complaints linked to the Baoro-Bouar road works. Of those, 1,289 were reviewed by committees and 61 were not yet reviewed because of the conflict that broke out in the country in December 2020; the report says those 61 would be handled by the project coordination unit and that if payment was needed the project could pay through a rural connectivity project. About 518 complaints were validated and notified to the enterprise for compensation in money or in kind. Of those 518, 429 were about houses cracking from vibration and the remaining 89 were for other damage, including trees and animals. Of the 89 complaints due financial compensation, 51 had received it, totalling FCFA 2,168,000, and 48 were still waiting for a total of FCFA 2,425,500. The report gives no figure for what the 429 house-cracking complaints received. In Cameroon, the report says all complaints received were about the loss of a piece of land to road works using machinery, and that all were processed and closed. In Chad, complaint management was handled by the project implementation unit and no complaint was received. The project reported six occupational health and safety incidents in Cameroon since the start of works, two classified as severe, two as serious and two as indicative, all accounted for through the Bank's incident reporting tool and closed, with a safeguards corrective action plan prepared and implemented; a footnote records a fatal accident in Cameroon in September 2019, for which an action plan was designed to mitigate such risks, and an incident involving an overloaded truck in the Central African Republic on 21 July 2019, classified as indicative. Two gender-based violence cases were reported to the Bank in Cameroon in September and November 2019, were handled under the project's protocol with follow-up by a specialist organisation, and were closed with disciplinary action taken under the code of conduct so that both perpetrators no longer worked for the project; in the Central African Republic a gender-based violence allegation on the Baoro-Bouar works was reported through the media, the case documentation was reviewed and the case was also closed. On safeguards, the report says performance was moderately unsatisfactory for an extended period: in Cameroon because the reforestation on the Mora-Dabanga-Kousseri section did not take place as planned in quantity or quality and because the Army Corps of Engineers did not fully comply with labour law on civilian staff; in Chad because there was no environmental and social audit to assess those aspects, and because of waste management and disposal problems on the new customs building site, for which the subcontractor agreed to remove waste from the riverside to a certified public site agreed with district authorities and to build a waterproof slab before final delivery; and in the Central African Republic because the abrupt halt to construction of the Baoro-Bouar road meant the stone quarries and borrow pits were not rehabilitated before closure.
baoro-bouar-road-house-damage-car.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,489 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated on any of the project's road sections. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the completion report gives no details on whether there was land acquisition, involuntary resettlement or any issue with the physical cultural resources safeguards, while noting that the appraisal document had said road widening on the Cameroonian section would involve land acquisition along the Benoue National Park and that several tombs were to be moved.
baoro-bouar-road-house-damage-car.killed_note: The completion report records in a footnote that a fatal accident occurred in Cameroon in September 2019 and that an action plan was designed and was being implemented to mitigate such risks. The footnote is attached to the report's count of six occupational health and safety incidents on the project in Cameroon since the start of works, all of which the report says were accounted for through the Bank's incident reporting tool and closed, so the death was on works the credit financed: the report records that the Mora-Dabanga and Dabanga-Kousseri road works contracts in the Far North were funded under the project and that they were being carried out by the Army Corps of Engineers under the project's restructuring at the time. The report does not name the person, does not say what happened, and does not say which road section or which contractor was involved. The death was in Cameroon, not on the Baoro-Bouar section in the Central African Republic where the complaints were registered. The death is not counted in this map's figure. The rule is that a death counts only where a document gives a cause tying it to the works, and this report gives none: it records that a fatal accident occurred and not what happened. The same rule leaves ten fatalities uncounted on the Metolong dam card and three on the Nigeria erosion card, and counts three on the Serbian Corridor X card, where the completion report attributes them to unsatisfactory management of site safety.
baoro-bouar-road-house-damage-car.outcome: The last credits closed on 28 February 2021, eight years after the original closing date, with financing cancelled twice in the final year. On the Bank's own figures, 48 of the 89 Baoro-Bouar complaints due money were still unpaid, FCFA 2,425,500 in total, and 61 of the 1,350 complaints had not been reviewed because of the conflict that broke out in December 2020; responsibility for those 61 was left after closing to the project coordination unit, with payment if needed to come through a separate rural connectivity project. The report states in its account of what affected implementation that the Baoro-Bouar works were not completed at the time of project closure, after 34 months of work against the 20 planned, and that the abrupt halt to the construction meant the stone quarries and borrow pits were not rehabilitated before closure; its economic analysis lists the same 56 kilometre section among five road sections completed at project closing. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that its cumbersome regulations and methodology for land valuation were one of the three reasons the completion report gives for the substantial delays in paying compensation, and that its involvement, together with changes to the road design and alignment during the works, led to the resettlement action plan being amended and more affected people being added.

agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.community: The credits paid for rebuilding about 110 kilometres of the Abidjan-Lagos coastal corridor in Ghana, from Agona Junction to Elubo at the border with Cote d'Ivoire, together with shorter sections in Benin and Togo. The Independent Evaluation Group's review lists the project's social impacts as changes in road alignment, loss of residential houses, loss of businesses, loss of temporary structures and increased noise and dust. Resettlement action plans were prepared for each country and disclosed before appraisal, each with a grievance and redress procedure, and counterpart funding was secured at appraisal to make sure affected people were fully compensated before civil works began. The affected-person figures the review gives are the appraisal's. The appraisal document of 25 February 2010 states, at paragraph 97 and again in its safeguards annex, that the number of project-affected persons was 101 households, 404 people, in Benin, with cash compensation costed at FCFA 171,046,800, about US$400,000; 379 households, 1,920 people, in Togo, costed at FCFA 879,073,630, about US$2.1 million, of which FCFA 149,793,795, about US$357,000, was cash compensation and FCFA 725,279,835, about US$1.7 million, civil works; and 744 households, 2,094 people, in Ghana, costed at about US$7.8 million in cash compensation. The review repeats those three figures without saying they are the plan's. Compensation was carried out in all three countries, but with prolonged delays in Ghana. The review then states that the Ghanaian government compensated 2,094 affected people in December 2012, before the civil works started, in line with the resettlement action plan - the same number the appraisal had planned for. Changes to the design and road alignment during the works, and the involvement of the Land Valuation Board, then led to the plan being amended and more affected people being added; the review states that the completion report does not give those figures. The completion report gives three reasons for the substantial delays in paying compensation: Ghana's cumbersome regulations and methodology for land valuation by the Land Valuation Board; heavy bureaucracy in the administration in allocating, approving and transferring money for compensation payments; and lengthy and difficult procedures for paying compensation under Ghanaian regulations. At project closing on 30 June 2017 the involuntary resettlement policy was not complied with, because approximately 11 per cent of affected people still had to be paid. The review records that the Bank team closely supervised safeguards implementation throughout, reported the issues in implementation status reports and downgraded the safeguards performance ratings, and that only at the end of the implementation period did it bring in a dedicated safeguards consultant to help the implementing agency; the compensations were then completed within a month of the closing date and the review states that full implementation of the resettlement action plan was achieved in August 2017. The project team told the Independent Evaluation Group that the resettlement action plan in Ghana had recently been amended in 2017 when the number of affected people reached 5,416, with compensation estimated at GHC 24.8 million, about US$5.6 million, and that as of 28 August 2017, 5,396 of them, about 99.5 per cent, had been fully compensated with only 20 left to be paid, after which the remaining people were able to collect their compensation at the Ghana Highway Authority's offices. In Togo the completion report considered the carrying out of the resettlement plan best practice. In Benin it reported serious concerns with the implementation of both environmental and social measures. On environmental safeguards in Ghana, which the project team rated Moderately Satisfactory, some borrow pits had been reinstated while others were left open at the request of owners who wanted to develop those areas further, structures at camp sites were in the care of local communities and needed cleaning up before the defects liability period closed, and a large depression left by rock extraction at the quarry site had turned into a lake needing protection measures.
agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,252 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The figures in the Independent Evaluation Group's review - 744 households, 2,094 people, in Ghana, 101 households, 404 people, in Benin and 379 households, 1,920 people, in Togo - are the appraisal document's own plan figures, printed at paragraph 97 and in its safeguards annex of 25 February 2010, and the review reprints them without saying so. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated in any of the three countries, and the review states that the completion report does not give the figures for the extra affected people added when the plan was amended during the works.
agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.outcome: The credits closed on 30 June 2017, nine months late, with the involuntary resettlement policy not complied with because approximately 11 per cent of affected people in Ghana were still unpaid. The Bank kept monitoring the payments after closing and the Independent Evaluation Group's review states that full implementation of the resettlement action plan was achieved in August 2017. The project team told the Independent Evaluation Group that by 28 August 2017, 5,396 of 5,416 affected people had been fully compensated with 20 remaining, and that those 20 could then collect their compensation at the Ghana Highway Authority's offices.

agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.confidence_note: This rests on one document. The Bank's own completion report for this project is not disclosed: it is not returned by the Bank's document interface under this project number, nor under the second-phase number, nor by a title search, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it is the only route to its findings. The review quotes the report by paragraph for the 11 per cent of affected people unpaid at closing and for the three reasons for the delay, so that finding is the lender's own account of its own project, at one remove. The affected-person counts the review gives are not outcomes at all: 744 households and 2,094 people for Ghana, 101 households and 404 people for Benin and 379 households and 1,920 people for Togo all appear word for word in the appraisal document of 25 February 2010, which costed the Ghana plan at about US$7.8 million in cash compensation. The approximately 11 per cent left unpaid at closing is the only outcome finding in the document, and no number of people is attached to it. The figures for the later position - 5,416 affected people, GHC 24.8 million, 5,396 compensated and 20 remaining as of 28 August 2017 - are not in any document: the review attributes them to information the project team gave the Independent Evaluation Group, and says the detail is in the last implementation status report. No independent account of the compensation delays on this road was found. A coalition of more than 7,000 farmers, landowners and property developers was reported by the Ghanaian Times on 18 August 2026 to be demanding compensation on the Elubo to Agona Nkwanta section, but that is Lot 1 of a later Abidjan-Lagos corridor road project, nine years after this credit closed, and no source found links it to this credit. No document found names any affected person, says how many people the 11 per cent amounted to, or says how long any individual waited to be paid. The review states that compensation was completed within a month of the closing date and that full implementation of the resettlement plan was achieved in August 2017. It prints no date on its pages; the 27 February 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is unverified at document level.
agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.conditions: The project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Cultural Property (OP/BP 4.11). An environmental and social impact assessment with an environmental management plan, and resettlement action plans, were prepared for each of the three countries and publicly disclosed before appraisal; each plan specified a grievance and redress procedure. Ghana's resettlement action plan for the Agona Junction to Elubo road was disclosed in November 2009, with addenda and an updated plan disclosed in April 2012 and December 2012. Counterpart funding was secured at the appraisal stage to ensure affected people would be fully compensated before civil works started, and in Ghana 2,094 people were paid in December 2012 before the works began. Changes to the design and alignment during the works, with the Land Valuation Board's involvement, required the plan to be amended and more affected people added, and at closing the involuntary resettlement policy was not complied with because approximately 11 per cent of affected people were still unpaid. Conformed financing and project agreements for Ghana's credit 4695-GH were signed on 5 August 2010 and for Benin's credit 4696-BJ on 8 April 2010 (Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, citing the Implementation Completion and Results Report at paragraphs 71 and 82; Project Appraisal Document, 25 February 2010).
agona-elubo-corridor-compensation-ghana.status_reason: Dropped on the documents. The completion report is undisclosed, so the Independent Evaluation Group's review is the only route to it, and the review holds no outcome count of harm. Its only outcome finding is that at closing the involuntary resettlement policy was not complied with because approximately 11 per cent of project-affected people still had to be paid: a percentage with no number of people attached and no denominator in any document. The affected-person counts it prints - Ghana 744 households and 2,094 persons, Benin 101 and 404, Togo 379 and 1,920 - are the appraisal document's plan figures, reproduced word for word from paragraph 97 and the safeguards annex of 25 February 2010 without attribution, which is BRIEF21 rule 2 at one remove; the resettlement action plan of November 2009 shows that the Ghana figure of 744 is in fact a count of fully and partially affected building structures, 231 permanent and 513 temporary, which the appraisal restated as 744 households. The later figures - 5,416 affected people, GHC 24.8 million, 5,396 compensated and 20 remaining as of 28 August 2017 - are prefaced 'The project team provided following additional information to IEG' and are a staff statement, not a document. Neither limb of the forward rule is met: limb (a) fails because no document counts anyone relocated, the 2,094 paid in December 2012 being a payment count equal to the plan figure; limb (b) fails because the only recorded shortfall is a percentage, with no count of people, no named person, no sum outstanding and no date by which anyone was still unpaid. The review also records that compensation was completed within a month of closing and that full implementation of the plan was achieved in August 2017.

lenders_add.role: The Kenya Transport Sector Support Project (P124109) closed on 31 December 2020. The completion report of 29 January 2021 rated social safeguards performance Moderately Unsatisfactory at close and listed four areas of non-compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy: the original engineering design for the interchanges was not based on minimising resettlement, so design updates during implementation disrupted the resettlement action plans and produced many resettlement complaints; the road corridors were not clear and free of encumbrances and compensation of affected people was not completed before the works began; carrying out the resettlement plans was lengthy and delayed, because of the design updates and insufficient government counterpart budget for compensation; and there was no well-funded, systematic stakeholder engagement or grievance process at the start. Environmental assessment was downgraded from Satisfactory to Moderately Satisfactory in November 2018 over poor management of quarry and borrow sites, health and safety risks and incidents at construction sites, community complaints about drainage and lack of access to residential homes, and the Inspection Panel case on the Webuye interchange; the rating was retained at Moderately Satisfactory in December 2019. The completion report records that on the major road contracts contractors mobilised before affected people had been compensated for land, property or business, so contractors could not take full possession of the sites, which slowed the works and had the Government paying for idle equipment and staff, and that this happened even though the safeguard instruments had been finalised well before the works began. At the time the report was written, rehabilitation of materials sites and compensation of affected people were still continuing, and the Bank told the Government it would remain engaged until all safeguards activities were complete (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 January 2021).

fields_add.community: The Bank's completion report of 29 January 2021 sets out the audit finding the Panel relied on and adds the rest of the project's record. The audit of the Webuye interchange resettlement action plan revealed 13 small business tenants who had not been included in the plan, and recommended cash compensation of KES 20,000 each for loss of income and relocation or disturbance, computed as an average of three months of net income; all 13 mobile traders received that payment in April 2020. It also recommended building a market for the 52 mobile traders omitted from the 2011 plan; the Government committed to build it, the land was identified and the engineering design was in progress when the report was written. Three other road sections drew complaints to the Bank's grievance service. On the Kakamega to Webuye section a complainant alleged a fatal accident involving a worker on site, dog attacks on workers in the contractor's camp, sexual exploitation and abuse of school girls by workers, and summary dismissal of workers who raised grievances. A Bank mission confirmed that there had been a fatal accident on site involving the operator of an excavator, that it had been reported to the police at the time, that the police took over the case, and that the Bank team followed up with the roads authority to ensure the family of the deceased was compensated under Kenyan law. It confirmed that the contractor kept five dogs for security, that they had roamed freely in the camp until workers complained and were then locked in kennels, and that one worker had been bitten and was treated at a local hospital. The allegation of sexual exploitation was investigated and could not be substantiated: the report records that children's officers, heads of schools and community leaders all said there had been no reports of abuse of children by workers. The allegation of summary dismissals could not be confirmed and the report says it appeared not to be true, since no member of the grievance committee or employee of the consultant or contractor who was interviewed knew of a worker dismissed for complaining. On the Athi River to Machakos section, compensation of affected people at the Gimu interchange was delayed while government agencies authenticated who was eligible, after the corridor was realigned to fit both the Standard Gauge Railway and the road widening and avoid double payment; some affected people complained to the Bank and that case was still open when the report was written. On the Bachuma Gate to Maji ya Chumvi contract one person's compensation was held in an escrow account with the National Land Commission while two families disputed ownership of the parcel in court. A further request for inspection on the project was submitted to the Inspection Panel and was not registered; the Panel issued a notice of non-registration on 13 April 2022.
